source: NaCCA Creative Arts Curriculum for Primary Schools (Basic 1–3), September 2019; indicator themes and exemplars grounded in the supplied curriculum
accessibility: Prompts may be read aloud. Accept oral, written, drawing, movement or demonstration responses when appropriate. Do not require personal religious or cultural disclosure, travel, purchases, or public performance. Use teacher-provided local examples; assess learning rather than access to resources.
note: 20 items are provided for each indicator below. The available curriculum passages substantiate the listed learning areas and exemplar themes; where the PDF's full indicator text was not retrievable, statements are framed as curriculum-aligned themes rather than quoted verbatim.

indicators.statement: Think about local people and describe their history, culture or way of life.
questions: Which can help us learn about local history?
A reliable story from a knowledgeable community member
Name one feature of a community's way of life.
Language, food, clothing, buildings, tools, songs or dances
Give one polite question about local history.
A respectful question about origins, leaders or traditions
Which is a visual artwork found in a community?
Name one local object that could inspire an artwork.
Basket, pot, textile, building or another verified example
You are unsure whether a cultural detail is accurate. What should you do?
Ask the teacher or use a reliable source
Which can show how people lived in the past?
Draw a community place based on a teacher-provided example.
Name one person who may share community knowledge.
Elder, artist, family member or teacher-approved resource person
How can you show respect when listening to a story?
Listen, wait your turn and ask politely
Why may communities have different customs?
Name one way stories are shared.
A learner describes an unfamiliar custom. What is a respectful response?
Listen without mocking and ask politely
What could a traditional tool tell us?
Name one way to record information you learn.
Notes, a drawing or a teacher-approved recording
Practise asking an artist or elder one respectful question.
Name one kind of visual art made in a community.
Drawing, pot, basket, carving, textile or poster
Tell or draw two facts about a teacher-provided local example.
Why should cultural differences be treated respectfully?
They are part of people's identity and heritage

indicators.statement: Think about and describe visual artworks made or found in the local community.
questions: Name one visual artwork found locally.
Pot, basket, poster, carving, textile or drawing
Name one material used in visual art.
Clay, paper, wood, fabric or safe found material
Match: pot; poster; basket to: holds items; shares a message; woven container.
Describe two features of a pictured artwork.
Relevant features such as colour, shape, line or texture
Draw a simple object used in your community.
How a surface feels or looks
You see an artwork you do not know. What can you do?
Observe and ask a respectful question
Which can be made by weaving?
Give one possible use of a locally made artwork.
Carry, store, wear, decorate or communicate
Which tool is used to draw?
Name one visual feature you can identify.
Line, shape, colour, size or texture
How might an artwork show community culture?
Through patterns, materials, symbols or uses
An artwork is fragile. How should you handle it?
Which is a safe classroom art tool?
Match: line; colour; shape with a visual feature description.
Identify a pictured artwork and describe its likely material or use.
Why should artworks be handled carefully?

indicators.statement: Reflect on how visual artworks show the natural environment.
questions: Which is part of the natural environment?
Name one natural object artists may observe.
Leaf, stone, animal, cloud or flower
Which feature can be observed in a stone?
Match: leaf; cloud; stone to: veins; changing form; hard surface.
Describe the shape or colour of a natural object.
What can nature inspire an artist to make?
Draw a natural object and include two details.
How can you observe a plant without harming it?
Look, draw or photograph it with permission
Any accurate colour observed in nature
A design with repeated lines, shapes or colours
How do natural forms inspire art?
Their colours, shapes, lines or textures give ideas
What is a safe way to collect ideas outdoors?
Observe or sketch without damaging living things
You want a flower for a drawing. What is a good choice?
Draw it in place or use a teacher-provided image
Name one shape found in nature.
Curved, oval, round or another observed shape
Match: shiny; rough; soft to surface descriptions.
Show a drawing inspired by nature and name one feature.
Why should we care for plants and animals?
They are living parts of the environment
Give one way nature can inspire a repeated design.
Repeat leaf, flower, wave or other observed forms

indicators.statement: Explore visual artworks that reflect topical issues in the local community.
questions: Which issue could an artwork show?
Name a community issue an artwork could communicate.
Litter, flooding, road safety or a teacher-provided topic
What might a road-safety poster show?
A picture shows a blocked drain. What concern might it represent?
How can an image help people notice an issue?
Which can be used to make a poster?
Name one action that reduces litter.
Use a bin or keep rubbish until one is available
What is a helpful purpose of issue-based art?
Share information or encourage positive action
A poster blames a group without evidence. How can it be improved?
Focus on the issue and helpful action
What might a picture of a clear drain communicate?
Keep drains clear or dispose of waste properly
Match: litter; unsafe crossing; dirty water with a helpful action.
Use a bin; cross carefully; protect water
Suggest a respectful slogan for a clean-up poster.
Name one way to make a poster clear.
Simple image, readable lettering or strong contrast
You have no personal example of an issue. What can you use?
Explain a poster's message to a classmate.
Sketch an artwork showing a safe community action.
Why should community artwork avoid insulting people?
Respectful messages are more helpful and fair

indicators.statement: Plan visual artworks based on local history, culture or way of life.
questions: What should an artist decide before making an artwork?
Name one local feature an artwork could represent.
A verified object, place, custom or activity
What can an outline help an artist plan?
A quick drawing used to develop an idea
You plan an artwork about a local celebration. What could you decide first?
Subject, key details and suitable materials
Sketch one idea for a local culture artwork.
Match: idea; material; sketch with: subject; what to use; quick plan drawing.
Name one material for a drawing.
Describe what your planned artwork will show.
You are unsure of a cultural detail. What should you do?
Check with the teacher or a reliable source
Use accurate details and avoid stereotypes
Name one community object that could inspire a picture.
A basket, pot, textile or building
Add one detail that helps show the setting.
Name one feature you could change in a plan.
When can an artwork plan be changed?
When a better idea or solution appears
Explain the subject and material for a planned artwork.
Your sketch is unclear. What could you do?
Add details or try another outline
How can art show community identity?
By including accurate local objects, patterns or places
Give one reason for a choice in your plan.
Relevant reason linked to subject or material

indicators.statement: Develop ideas and choose tools, materials and methods for making visual artworks.
questions: Which tool can colour a drawing?
Paper, pencil, crayon or clean reusable material
Clay can be used for what?
You plan a paper collage. What materials might you need?
Match: pencil; crayon; clay with drawing; colouring; modelling.
To suit the idea and method
How can you make a simple pattern?
Repeat a line, shape or colour
Make an outline for a planned artwork.
A tool seems sharp or unfamiliar. What should you do?
Ask the teacher and use only with permission
Follow instructions and share tools carefully
Explain why a material fits your artwork idea.
What does modelling mean in art?
Shaping material to make a form
Which method can make a basket?
Match: cut paper; shape clay; draw lines with collage; modelling; drawing.
Name one clean material that could be reused.
A colour is unavailable. What can you do?
Choose an available colour or ask the teacher
Choose a tool and demonstrate safe handling.
Why put tools away after art time?
To keep people safe and tools ready
Name one material or method you chose and why.

indicators.statement: Explore ideas and methods for creating performances about the natural and man-made local environment.
questions: Name one man-made feature a performance might show.
Which instrument can make a sound in a performance?
Name one safe sound source for a class performance.
Plan a movement showing a tree in wind. What could you do?
Describe one sound from the natural environment.
A suitable example such as rain or birds
What can a drama show about a community?
Match: rain; traffic; bird to natural or man-made sound source.
Name one movement that could show flowing water.
A performance needs a loud sound. How can the class keep it safe?
Use a moderate volume and teacher guidance
What can performers use to create rhythm?
Name one way to show a building through movement.
Use still shapes or pretend to open a door
Act out caring for a community garden.
An artwork shared through actions, sound or movement
To organise ideas and keep actions safe
Match: voice; body movement; prop to singing; dance; visual support.
A learner does not want to perform in front of everyone. What is an alternative?
Offer a small-group, spoken, written or behind-the-scenes role
Create a short movement sequence inspired by a natural feature.
Movement relates to the chosen feature
Name one man-made sound in a community.
Bell, vehicle or other suitable example
Explain how performance can express an idea about a place.
Links movement or sound to a place

indicators.statement: Choose performing arts resources and methods for expressing a topical community issue.
questions: Which could communicate a safety message?
Name one community issue a performance could address.
Litter, road safety or teacher-provided concern
What can a shaker provide in a performance?
Name one method for sharing a message through performance.
A group wants to show keeping the area clean. What action might they perform?
Put litter in a bin or clean safely
State one message a performance could share.
Why choose resources that suit the performance?
Match: clapping; spoken words; movement to rhythm; dialogue; dance.
How can a performance show road safety?
Act out careful crossing in a safe space
A scene includes a risky action. How can it be changed?
Use a safe pretend action or mime
Let's care for our shared space
Name one simple prop that could support a performance.
Practise a short dialogue encouraging safe behaviour.
What should performers do before using an instrument?
Why should an issue performance avoid blaming people unfairly?
It should be accurate and respectful
Match issue to message: litter; unsafe crossing; water pollution.
Use a bin; cross carefully; protect water
The group has no instrument. What can create rhythm?
Plan a short, safe performance about a helpful community action.
Name one way to include someone who prefers not to act.
Offer narrator, sound, design or planning role
Explain why you chose a particular sound or movement.

indicators.statement: Create a performance reflecting local history, culture or way of life.
questions: Which can be part of a performance?
Name one source for a local performance idea.
Teacher-provided story, song, dance or community account
Which instrument can accompany a dance?
Name one safe way to make a rhythm.
Your class creates a dance based on a verified local example. What should you consider?
Match: drum; shaker; whistle to possible sound source.
A clear repeated or changing movement
Perform or demonstrate a simple repeated movement pattern.
Why should local performance ideas be treated respectfully?
They represent people and their culture
Act a short everyday scene based on a teacher-provided community story.
Name one way a song can show local life.
Words or rhythm may describe activities or places
You do not know a traditional movement. What should you do?
Ask the teacher or use a provided demonstration
Which prop is suitable only if clean and approved?
Match: beginning; middle; ending to performance sequence.
What is a cue in a performance?
A signal to start or change an action
Give one safe rule for dance movement.
Create a short sound-and-movement sequence inspired by a local way of life.
Why practise before sharing a performance?
To remember the sequence and coordinate
Name one role besides acting in a performance.
Narrator, rhythm keeper, designer or organiser

indicators.statement: Present performances to share ideas about local history and culture.
questions: What can a performance share with an audience?
Name one way to prepare before performing.
Practise, plan roles or check the space
What helps an audience hear a speaker?
A performer forgets a line. What can the group do?
Pause, prompt kindly or continue safely
Match: performer; audience; narrator with: shares action; watches/listens; tells events.
Why plan where performers will stand?
To make space and action clear and safe
Someone does not want to perform publicly. What can they do?
Take a voluntary support or small-group role
Name one way a performance can educate an audience.
Share accurate information or a positive lesson
Why should cultural performances use accurate details?
What can a simple prop help show?
Match: practise; cue; clear space to readiness; timing; safety.
The space is crowded. What should performers do?
Stop and ask the teacher to arrange a safe space
Present a short spoken, movement or sound piece to a small group.
How can an audience respond kindly to a beginner?
What should be done after a performance?
Thank the audience and put materials away
Name one thing you learned by sharing a performance.

indicators.statement: Appreciate and discuss own and others' artworks using simple observations.
questions: Which is a kind way to discuss someone's artwork?
I like the colours you chose
Name one feature to observe in an artwork.
Colour, line, shape, texture or subject
Describe one thing you notice in an artwork.
Looking carefully and sharing a thoughtful response
A kind specific observation or suggestion
You do not understand an artwork. What can you do?
Ask the artist what they intended
Match: subject; material; colour to what is shown; what it is made from; visible hue.
Name one question you could ask an artist.
What idea or material did you use?
The repeated shapes make a clear pattern
A classmate's artwork differs from yours. What is appropriate?
Respect the difference and discuss a feature
It helps people learn without hurting feelings
Circle or point to one feature you like in a pictured artwork.
Name one material you think an artwork uses.
Match: rough; smooth; repeated to texture or pattern description.
What is one way to improve an artwork?
Add detail, adjust shape or try another colour
Someone gives a suggestion you do not want to use. What can you do?
Give one positive observation and one gentle question about an artwork.
Why look carefully before giving feedback?
To make comments specific and fair
What can you learn by looking at different artworks?
